https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/08/01/nirm.text: Menü Kereső Meghalt Nirmal Purja neves nepáli hegymászó tíz másik emberrel együtt egy lavinában Külföld Ignácz Péter Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Meghalt Nirmal Purja brit-nepáli hegymászó, a brit különleges erők egykori tagja, amikor lavina sodorta el az általa vezetett expedíciót a Pakisztánban található Broad Peak hegycsúcsra – közölte az Elite Exped nevű cég, aminek társalapítója volt. „Mélységes szomorúsággal erősítjük meg, hogy Nirmal Purja életét vesztette a Broad Peaken történt lavinaomlás következtében. Arról is megerősítést kaptunk, hogy az expedíció többi tagja sem élte túl a szerencsétlenséget” – írta a cég. Korábbi jelentések szerint a 8051 méter magas Broad Peaken történt lavinaomlásban tíz hegymászó – hat nepáli, egy pakisztáni, egy ománi, egy amerikai és egy kínai állampolgár – tűnt el csütörtökön. A 43 éves Nirmal Purja a szerencsétlenül járt expedíció vezetője volt. Egy pénteki tájékoztatás szerint keresőakció indult az eltűntek után, miután a hegymászók elvesztették a kapcsolatot az alaptáborukkal a lavina után. A rossz időjárás nehezítette a mentési munkálatot, amelyben katonai helikopterek is részt vettek. Purja azután vált világhírűvé, hogy 2019-ben alig több mint hat hónapon belül megmászta az összes nyolcezres csúcsot, később pedig ő vezette azt a csapatot, ami először mászta meg télen a világ második legmagasabb hegycsúcsát, a K2-t. Halálhírére reagált a nepáli kormányfő is, aki közölte, hogy a „hat nepáli és négy másik külföldi hegymászó, köztük a világcsúcstartó Nirmal Purja tragikus halála a pakisztáni Karakoram hegységben megrendített minket”, hozzátéve, hogy „bátorságuk, elkötelezettségük és hozzájárulásuk története mindig inspiráló marad”. A brit védelmi miniszter az X közösségi oldalon közzétett posztjában közölte, hogy „hihetetlen szomorúsággal tölt el Niram (Nims) Purja és mászótársai halála”, közölve, hogy „inspiráló ember volt, aki évekig szolgált a fegyveres erőinknél – és akinek hihetetlen hegymászó kalandjai az egész világon ismertek.” Purja élete azonban nem volt botrányoktól mentes. A róla szóló 2024-es cikkünket itt tudják elolvasni. Kedvenceink Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Kövess minket Facebookon is! Követem! https://isp.netscape.com:443/news/world/.text: News Home U.S. World Entertainment Money Politics Sports Science Health Odd News A punishing European drought shrivels crops from Dutch potatoes to Bosnian corn WOLPHAARTSDIJK, Netherlands (AP) — A cloud of dust billows behind Maarten Janse’s tractor as he spreads a mixture of compost, straw and manure over a field to nourish the parched soil. Janse's farm on the fertile land of the Netherlands' southwestern Zeeland Province is drying out despite his efforts to make it more drought resistant as accelerated human-caused global warming and a supersized El Nino batter fields across Europe. The drought that is roasting much of Europe this summer is taking a heavy toll on crops across the continent, from potatoes in the Netherlands to corn in Bosnia and grapes in Italy . Even when farmers try to adapt, the extreme weather is hitting their crops and water supplies. Triodos, a Dutch bank that has a focus on sustainability, published an analysis this week that estimated the heatwaves and drought could reduce gross domestic product across the European Union by 1% for 2026 or around 180 billion euros ($208 billion). Farmers are among the hardest hit, with their crops set to be badly affected by soaring temperatures and lack of water. In large parts of the Netherlands, farmers are no longer allowed to use water from streams and drainage channels to irrigate fields and orchards. Another farmer in Zeeland, Hendrik Jan ten Cate, looks at a field full of withered potato plants that are almost all ready for harvest — a month early and with a significantly reduced crop. His potatoes are used to make French fries for companies including McDonald’s, but they’re likely going to be too small this year. “People want long fries,” he says as he holds one of the potatoes. “That’s going to be tough this year.” Ten Cate is one of the lucky farmers because he is allowed to irrigate his crops. But, even so, he estimates his harvest this year will be down by about one-third compared to average years. “It's not just the drought that is the problem,” he says. “It is also the sun, the dry air and especially the hot days we have had this year. The potatoes just can't handle that combination very well.” In Bosnia, where agriculture contributes roughly 5% of annual GDP and 10% of all employment, grain farmer Slavisa Lukic stood in one of his corn fields as stalks blew limply in the breeze. His crops have been hit by repeated heat waves and drought conditions. He said this year’s corn yield would be very poor, if he manages to harvest one at all. Lukic remembers when he grew 6 to 7 tons per hectare on his farm. He expects this year’s corn yield will be around 1.5 to 2 tons per hectare. Pointing to the drought-stricken land in northeastern Bosnia, Lukic said clover fields that once grew abundantly have all but disappeared. “Now they literally do not exist,” he said. “Nothing.” The drought is even hitting one of the Czech Republic's most famous products: beer. Plzeňský Prazdroj, the country’s largest beer producer, expects to incur losses this year due to a stunted hops yield. Jakub Zaoral, the brewer’s sustainability manager, said that changes in rainfall patterns — characterized by long periods of dryness with occasional heavy storms — mean that when rain does fall, it runs off the dry soil. That results in inconsistent yields and increasingly low groundwater levels. “There’s no choice but to simply accept the fact that one year will be great and the next won’t be,” he said. “If it were to happen three times in a row, that could very well become an existential problem for hop growers.” In Romania, some heat and drought-resistant crops like sunflowers have been less affected by the extreme conditions and yields have been plentiful. But the drought is still hitting home with record-low water levels on the Danube River disrupting grain transport, causing chronically congested terminals and an increasing pileup of crops with nowhere to go. “In a short time, maximum 10 days, we will enter full blast in sunflower harvest, to be followed by corn,” Cezar Gheorghe, founder of grain consultancy firm Agricolumn, told The Associated Press. “Already farmers are in panic mode. They can’t find a place to store the corn and sunflower seeds.” Cattle grazing plains in Hungary are turning to dust. No rain has fallen on Sándor Molnár's dairy farm since late May and he is having to buy expensive feed for his 130 cows. “We’re trying to hang in there and hope for the best, hoping next year will be better,” he added. “To be honest, we’ve been saying that for a few years now, but maybe this time it will be.” Elveden Estate, with more than 10,000 acres of farmland on the Suffolk-Norfolk border in eastern England, has built a reservoir that can hold enough water to fill about 200 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Less than a year after opening, it's almost dry. Another reservoir is at about 20% capacity. But the farm's water policy is paying off. “The fact that we’ve invested significantly in reservoir storage and the infrastructure associated with pumping water has meant that we’ve been in a very strong position to continue to irrigate our crops through this growing season,” the farm's managing director, Andrew Blenkiron, said. But every drop counts. “We’re very concerned that we haven’t got enough water to see us through this season,” Blenkiron said. “We’ve got probably, if this weather stays as it is, six weeks of watering left to do.” Janse uses no-till farming on his fields — not plowing the soil, planting crops to cover the ground year-round and adding organic matter — to help cope with the whims of the weather as climate change triggers more extremes. He has also diversified by running a popular campsite on his farm near the picturesque town of Veere. As he tends to his fields, guests walk by toward a lake where yachts and a river cruise ship sail past. And as dry weather causes an increase in soil salinity in fields, Janse grows samphire, also known as sea asparagus, on a small patch of land. It's a crop that can thrive in salty conditions. But with no rainfall, even that is struggling this year. “Samphire needs fresh water, and if there is only saltwater it doesn’t grow either,” he said. ___ Nadja Lovadinov in London, Mustakim Hasnath in Suffolk, Stanislav Hodina in Prague, Czech Republic, Justin Spike in Budapest, Hungary, and Stephen McGrath in Leamington Spa, England, contributed to this report. 08/13/2026 04:28 -0400 © Copyright The Associated Press. https://www.politico.eu/article/uk-launc.text: LONDON — Andy Burnham’s government desperately wants to find ways to help Brits save money on soaring energy bills. The latest idea: Getting them to put mini solar panels on their balconies so they can generate their own power. From Thursday, the tech — already a success story in countries like Germany — will be available to buy in high street stores and install in U.K. properties for the first time. Plug-in solar panels are “a simple, affordable way for households to take control of their energy bills and start saving straight away,” Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said. But to get there, ministers face a clutch of problems, including uncooperative landlords, safety fears, and hundreds of pounds in upfront costs. Advertisement Advertisement Regulation, regulation, regulation The technology was badged as a simpler solution for renters or other people without space at home for traditional rooftop panels. People who want to install the kit may need permission from landlords, freeholders or councils, therefore. And some are already not playing ball. One housing association, Sovereign Network Group — which manages 86,000 homes across London and the south of England — said it has a blanket ban on letting residents install plug-in solar in the buildings it manages. “While solar panels may be installed through our planned retrofit programme, we do not permit plug-in or ‘plug and play’ solar panels in SNG properties,” said Carol Bailey, SNG’s building and occupational safety director, citing potential “electrical safety risks.” Claire Hibbit, corporate affairs director at another housing association in England, Notting Hill Genesis, which manages over 60,000 properties, said they wanted to help tenants use cleaner power — before listing all the hurdles tenants would need to clear before plugging in solar panels: ensuring they were bought from a reputable outlet, holding an electricity safety certificate, safe installation, no extra fire risk, the right weight for a balcony, and not breaking any rules governing conservation areas. A third, L&Q, which manages over 105,000 properties, said it welcomed the potential of plug-in panels to help cut bills. But its Director of Health and Building Safety Steve Pettitt added: “As this technology is new, we're still considering the detail, including how it can be used safely in residents’ homes.” Advertisement Advertisement “Plug-in solar panels send electricity in the opposite direction in your property’s wiring,” said Luke Osborne, technical director of the charity Electrical Safety First. His organization has “concerns plug-in solar panels may damage older devices in people's homes which protect people from electric shock,” he warned. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, who talked up the benefits of plug-in solar panels, arrives at 10 Downing Street for a cabinet meeting on July 21, 2026. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images Another trade association, the Electrical Contractors Association, warned ahead of the government's roll out that plug-in solar could “overload circuits — creating a risk of fire and electrical shocks — without careful checks by qualified electricians.” ‘Robust’ The government insisted plug-in solar is not intended for every home, and has been made legal only after “rigorous, independent safety testing,” using panels “safe and compatible with U.K. wiring.” “As a government, we are quite confident that the safety case is robust, and the additional work that we've done to assure ourselves of that is giving us the confidence to be able to legalize these in the U.K. and assure ourselves that they will be safe for people in their homes,” added Energy Minister Martin McCluskey. He said he had written to landlords to make the case for plug-in solar and hoped “that would be looked on favorably” by them. The government has flagged a detailed safety checklist as part of the roll-out. The government reckons that each piece of kit could produce enough power to cover 20 percent of average household energy use, according to an announcement from the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero Wednesday. Advertisement Advertisement Ministers said the “easy-to-install” panels could save homes up to £110 per year in energy bills, part of Andy Burnham’s effort to give people some “breathing space” on the cost of living. The promise came on the same day the regulator announced household energy bills are set to rise once again from October, driven up by the war between the U.S., Israel and Iran. Saving money (slowly) Plug-in solar panels also come with a hefty upfront price, even as the government promotes them as a way — over time — to save money. As of Wednesday, one U.K. online retailer, flagged by McCluskey as a potential provider of plug-in solar, had set the price for a piece of kit at £699. The government believes the price of a single panel will settle, thanks to market competition, between £400 and £600, the minister said. This means, as the U.K. heads into higher energy prices this fall, the £110 annual savings proposed off the back of plug-in solar would not help voters start recouping the costs until the end of the decade. McCluskey ruled out government support to cover the upfront costs of the tech, such as schemes that already exist for other clean power like heat pumps and larger-scale rooftop solar panels. Ministers could revisit the issue in the future, he added. Even at a higher price of between £500 and £700, the so-called “payback period” is “still lower than you would get from rooftop solar,” McCluskey later insisted. Advertisement Advertisement The push comes as worries grow about the impact of rising household energy bills. Data released this week by consumer group Citizens Advice showed more than 10 million British households are worried about how they'll afford their bills in the colder months ahead. The government must find a way to help people “trapped in cold, dark homes this winter,” urged Citizens Advice boss Claire Moriarty. Charlie Cooper contributed to this report.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6n4.text: Figure caption, Watch: Aerial footage shows riders stuck on Six Flags roller coaster By Sareen Habeshian Published 13 October 2026, 00:36 BST Updated 3 hours ago One person has died and several others were injured after an incident on a rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia, an amusement park in the US state of Georgia. The Cobb County Police Department said it was investigating the fatality at the park, about 15 miles (24km) from Atlanta, according to the BBC's news partner CBS. Police did not specify what ride was involved, but aerial footage from news helicopters showed the Goliath rollercoaster stopped midway, with riders being helped off by workers. Six Flags Over Georgia said it was "deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today. Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends, and loved ones." Officials have not said how the person was killed. The BBC has contacted local police and fire authorities, as well as park officials. Witnesses told local media they saw a man ejected from the ride, accounts that the BBC has not verified. Local outlet 11Alive quoted , external a witness saying the man fell from the rollercoaster on to the roof of a haunted house attraction. A park spokesperson said in a statement that its team and local authorities had responded immediately, and they were co-operating on an investigation into the incident. Mableton Mayor Michael Owens said the city's public safety director was co-ordinating with local police and park security on the situation. The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five. Six Flags is the largest amusement park operator in North America, with 20 amusement parks, 14 water parks and nine resorts across Canada, the US and Mexico. The incident comes just weeks after one of its parks in southern California announced it would close the popular X2 roller coaster after more than 100 people alleged brain injuries from the ride. Six Flags said the ride had passed a range of safety tests, but that it had decided to retire it because it was "the right thing to do".
